cards.b:
Food is too big to enter your blood. Digestion breaks it into tiny molecules that can. Knowing the steps explains acidity, lactose intolerance, why fibre matters and why malnutrition remains a big issue.

The gut is really a long tube, about 9 metres from mouth to anus, that is technically 'outside' the body. Food must be broken down twice over: mechanically (chewing, churning) and chemically (enzymes). Only then can the small molecules be absorbed: starch into glucose, protein into amino acids, and fat into fatty acids. William Beaumont studied digestion directly in the 1820s through a soldier's stomach wound.
The digestive tract is a long tube, about 9 metres, with helpers (liver, pancreas, gall bladder). Digestion is both mechanical (chewing, churning) and chemical (enzymes).

Salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars (chew roti long enough and it tastes sweet). The stomach makes hydrochloric acid (pH about 2) that kills germs, and pepsin that cuts proteins. A mucus layer protects the wall. William Beaumont studied digestion through a gunshot wound in Alexis St Martin's stomach in the 1820s.

Bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) breaks fat into droplets. The pancreas sends enzymes: amylase, trypsin and lipase. The wall makes more enzymes. The lining has finger-like villi that give a surface of roughly a tennis court for absorption of sugars, amino acids and fatty acids into blood and lymph.

It absorbs water and salts and forms faeces. Trillions of bacteria help make vitamin K and some B vitamins and break fibre. Gut microbes now link to immunity and mood.

The large intestine is about 1.5 metres long and takes the leftovers, mostly water, fibre and dead cells. It reclaims roughly a litre or more of water a day, which is why severe diarrhoea is dangerous: water is lost before it can be absorbed. Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells of the gut wall. Antibiotics can disturb this community, and a probiotic like curd may help restore it.

• Carbohydrates: main fuel.
  • Proteins: building and repair.
  • Fats: energy, cell membranes, vitamins A, D, E, K.
  • Vitamins and minerals: small amounts, big roles. Iron for blood; iodine for thyroid; vitamin D for bones.
  • Fibre and water.

Think of a balanced thali as a toolkit: rice or roti for fuel, dal for protein, vegetables for vitamins and fibre, and a little ghee or oil for fat-soluble vitamins. About 20 amino acids build our proteins, and nine are 'essential', meaning we must eat them. Iodised salt protects the thyroid, and milk, sunlight and fish give vitamin D. Water makes up about 60 percent of body weight.

Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy (James Lind showed lime helped sailors, 1747). Vitamin D lack gives rickets. Vitamin A lack leads to night blindness. Iron lack leads to anaemia. Protein-energy lack gives kwashiorkor and marasmus.

These diseases are the reverse of a well-planned diet. James Lind tested citrus fruit on sailors in 1747, in one of the first controlled trials, long before vitamin C was discovered. Anaemia is very common in India, especially among women and children, and is addressed with iron-folic acid tablets and fortified foods. Kwashiorkor, with swollen belly, comes from too little protein; marasmus, with wasting, from too little food overall.

Christiaan Eijkman (1890s) found that unpolished rice prevented beriberi in fowl; Frederick Hopkins and Casimir Funk worked on 'vital amines' in the 1910s. Ivan Pavlov (1890s) studied digestive reflexes. H. pylori, found by Marshall and Warren (1982), causes most stomach ulcers, not stress.

Eijkman's chickens fed polished rice developed a paralysis like beriberi, and brown rice cured them; Hopkins showed in 1912 that milk contained 'accessory food factors'. Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestive glands. Barry Marshall even drank a culture of H. pylori to prove his point, and he and Robin Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize. Ulcers are now treated with antibiotics.

Fix these

  • Ulcers are mainly from H. pylori and painkillers, not spicy food alone.
  • Most absorption is in the small intestine, not the stomach.
  • Fat is not 'bad'; the type and amount matter.

Also, 'acidity' is not always too much acid: stomach acid (pH about 1.5 to 2) is needed to kill germs and activate pepsin, and the stomach lining is protected by a layer of mucus. Digestion does not start in the stomach, either: salivary amylase starts on starch in the mouth. Fibre cannot be digested, but it keeps the gut moving.

India runs the Integrated Child Development Services (1975), Mid-Day Meal (now PM POSHAN) and the National Food Security Act (2013). Anaemia remains widespread among women and children. Iodised salt (National Goitre Control Programme, 1962) cut iodine deficiency. Millets are promoted as 'Shree Anna' after 2023, the International Year of Millets.

• Mouth, stomach, small and large intestine do different jobs.
  • Villi increase absorption area.
  • Enzymes: amylase (starch), pepsin and trypsin (protein), lipase (fat).
  • Deficiencies cause specific diseases.

Think about it:

  1. Why does bile not digest fat chemically but still help?
  2. Why do we need pH 2 in the stomach but not in the intestine?
